prompt: A model change lowers p95 from 3.0 seconds to 2.1 seconds. The same release raises critical-field extraction errors from 1.2% to 4.7%, above a 2% limit. What should the release owner conclude?

options.text: Average the latency and error improvements into one composite score and ship if it is positive.
Accept because p95 improved by 30% and the quality regression is small in absolute terms.
Reject the candidate until it meets the critical-field floor and full-route target.
Add retries until the extraction error rate returns below the limit without measuring added latency.

prompt: A report says the new route has 1.4-second p95, but it excludes requests that timed out after 2 seconds. The previous route completed 99.8% of requests. Which comparison should decide whether users received a faster service?

options.text: Compare p95 only among completed requests for both versions.
Compare provider model latency because timeouts are owned by the application.
Replace timeouts with the two-second threshold and compute p95 without reporting the count.
Compare end-to-end outcomes on all assigned requests, treating timeouts and missing completions explicitly alongside latency among completed requests.

prompt: Four independent lookups are currently serialized, followed by a verifier that needs all four results. Measurements show each lookup averages 300 ms and the verifier takes 500 ms; dependencies allow lookups to run concurrently. Which test is justified?

options.text: Parallelize the verifier with the lookups so the response starts earlier.
Parallelize independent lookups, then verify after all required results arrive.
Return the first lookup result and skip remaining sources when they are slow.
Run all calls sequentially because parallel execution always increases model uncertainty.

prompt: A route receives a transient 429 with a documented retry-after interval. Its client currently retries immediately twice, causing more 429s and breaching p95. What should the next experiment change?

options.text: Retry immediately more times to increase the chance that one call succeeds.
Retry every error once after the same fixed delay, including validation and authorization errors.
Honor retry-after with a bounded retry policy and compare full-route outcomes.
Disable all retries and count every transient 429 as a final failure.

prompt: A synchronous endpoint returns a progress message quickly, but downstream settlement requires a validated final result that can take 4 seconds. The consumer accepts either a complete response within 1 second or an approved asynchronous job acknowledged in 1 second and completed later. Which design meets the contract?

options.text: Use the approved async path and preserve final validation as the completion contract.
Stream provisional output and assume it counts as the one-second completed response.
Increase the synchronous timeout to four seconds without checking the consumer contract.
Return the progress message synchronously and label the operation complete.

prompt: A retry reduces missing responses but occasionally repeats a non-idempotent write after the first response is lost. The service has no idempotency key or status lookup. What is the safe next step?

options.text: Return success whenever the request was dispatched to avoid retries.
Retry with a new request ID so the service treats it as a new operation.
Retry only when the client receives no response within 500 ms.
Add service-supported idempotency or reconciliation before retrying unknown writes.

prompt: A candidate parallelizes two independent searches and lowers the median by 350 ms. It also increases provider throttling; p95 is unchanged, and the route remains within its 3-second target. What evidence should guide rollout?

options.text: Reject the candidate because any increase in 429 responses invalidates parallelism.
Compare resolution quality, completion, 429 recovery, tail latency, and cost on a representative workload, then expand only if the full contract remains satisfied.
Compare only first-token latency because both searches are independent and start together.
Roll out because the median improved and the p95 target still passes.

prompt: A streamed answer is cut off in the browser. Provider logs show a completed message, while the application database has no committed answer row. Which trace boundary should be added first?

options.text: Record only model completion latency because the provider reports success.
Log the full response body at every layer to compare copies later.
Correlate provider completion, gateway delivery, browser receipt, and durable commit as separate events for the same logical operation and attempt.
Assign a new unrelated trace ID to the database write and search by approximate timestamp.

prompt: An asynchronous agent workflow launches three workers. The parent times out and retries while the first workers continue. Current dashboards count five worker results but cannot tell which parent attempt owns them. What telemetry key change is needed?

options.text: Give every worker the parent’s single request ID and omit worker identifiers.
Link worker and parent attempts with task, source, and merge identifiers.
Use only each provider request ID because it is globally unique.
Assign a new workflow ID on every worker event.

prompt: A rare authorization denial occurs in 0.05% of tool calls. Head-based sampling keeps 1% of requests and almost never captures a denial. Operators need denial rate and latency distribution without storing request bodies. Which design is best to test?

options.text: Count denial events only and discard route, decision, and timing dimensions.
Raise global head sampling to 100% and store all prompts and tool arguments indefinitely.
Sample only successful tool calls more frequently to improve the latency estimate.
Keep a representative baseline sample and add a bounded event rule for denials with policy decision, operation, latency, and safe identifiers.

prompt: A tool call is retried after a timeout. The first attempt actually committed the action, but its response was lost; the retry is denied as a duplicate. Current traces label the whole operation ‘failed’. What should be changed?

options.text: Retry again with a new operation ID so the tool will accept it.
Mark the final attempt’s denial as the operation result and discard earlier attempts.
Report success as soon as the first attempt is dispatched.
Instrument material stages and compare their latency distributions on the route.

prompt: A legal review allows one operator to inspect a redacted excerpt for a specific incident. The telemetry store currently retains full prompts for every request. What is the proportionate adjustment?

options.text: Allow the operator to query any conversation for the same user while the incident is open.
Keep routine traces metadata-only and implement narrowly scoped, time-bounded, audited access to the approved redacted incident excerpt.
Retain all full prompts but encrypt the log bucket.
Delete every trace field, including latency and tool status.

prompt: A release changes prompt wording and retriever ranking together. Grounded-answer rate falls, but all traces contain only a combined ‘release version’ and no component versions. What minimum change enables useful attribution next time?

options.text: Use causal links and monotonic durations, while recording clock uncertainty.
Roll back both components after every regression and record only the deployment date.
Increase the number of full conversation logs without adding version fields.
Add a free-form operator note naming whichever component seems responsible.

prompt: A queue worker receives a task, retries it twice, and eventually finishes. The front-end trace ends at enqueue, so an incident report cannot separate queue delay from model latency. What should be propagated?

options.text: Carry trace context through enqueue and worker execution, with timestamps for enqueue, dequeue, attempts, tool/model stages, and completion.
Start a fresh trace in the worker and correlate it by user ID.
Record model latency and assume the remainder is queue overhead.
Measure only total wall-clock time from the browser.

prompt: A benchmark shows 99.9% transport success, but customers report incomplete final answers. The client receives deltas and may stop after a disconnect. Which additional outcome should the trace define?

options.text: Whether the stream reached its terminal completion event and whether the application assembled and delivered the expected final payload.
Use HTTP 200 as the completion signal for the whole answer.
Measure only the first-token latency because users saw some text.
Count any received text delta as a successful response.

prompt: A workflow dashboard says 100% of jobs succeeded because every queue message was acknowledged. A downstream worker can acknowledge before persisting its result. Which event should define completion?

options.text: Define completion at durable result commit, distinct from queue acknowledgment.
The first model response, because computation is complete then.
The absence of a retry message after one minute.
Queue acknowledgment, because it proves the worker received the task.

prompt: The platform records per-request spans, but a parent workflow fans out to agents and combines their answers. Operators can see each span but cannot tell which result fed a final claim. What trace relationship is missing?

options.text: A common user ID across all spans.
More detailed provider latency fields on every span.
A single free-text note written after the final answer.
Link synthesis spans to the worker results and evidence they consumed.

prompt: A service reports normal completion time but users say results arrive late. The trace has model start/end spans and one overall request duration; it has no retrieval or queue events. What instrumentation change would most directly isolate the delay?

options.text: Add queue, retrieval, tool, model, validation, and delivery spans.
Subtract model duration from overall duration and label the remainder as queue time.
Increase model sampling and compare completion tokens with the previous release.
Log the full user prompt and final answer with wall-clock timestamps for every request.

prompt: A worker’s clock is six minutes behind the API gateway. The trace viewer orders the worker result before the tool request that launched it, making the incident timeline look impossible. Which correction is most useful?

options.text: Discard worker events from cross-service traces until all machines have synchronized clocks.
Replace worker timestamps with the parent timestamp so every span appears in sequence.
Use trace links for causality and clock metadata for cross-service timestamps.
Sort events by local wall-clock timestamp and increase the viewer’s allowed skew window.

prompt: A maintenance corpus has 2,400 short, self-contained checklist steps and 70 long procedures with cross-page prerequisites. One fixed chunk size makes the short steps noisy and splits long procedures. Which first change should the team evaluate?

options.text: Keep the fixed chunking and increase top-k until both content types appear.
Segment by source structure, preserve prerequisites, and test both query classes.
Embed each sentence independently and let the answer model reconstruct every procedure.
Apply one much larger chunk size to the whole corpus so long procedures retain context.

prompt: A troubleshooting guide uses numbered steps, where step 4 applies only if step 2 returned code E17. Retrieval often returns step 4 without the condition. What indexing representation best preserves the rule?

options.text: Increase overlap uniformly by 50 tokens across all chunks.
Keep each prerequisite with its dependent step, or retrieve an explicit link with it.
Copy the entire guide into each chunk so every step has all context.
Index each step alone and rely on the model to infer the missing condition from numbering.

prompt: A contract repository contains tables whose columns are ‘effective date’, ‘notice period’, and ‘renewal rule’. Search returns the correct row text but omits its column labels. Which repair should be tried first?

options.text: Increase embedding dimensions so the row values carry more semantic signal.
Ask the model to infer the missing column from neighboring rows at answer time.
Index each table value with its column label and row identity.
Add the table title to every row and leave the columns out.

prompt: A bilingual safety manual has Polish and English passages aligned paragraph by paragraph. Users ask in either language, and current translated embeddings retrieve semantically related but sometimes different revision paragraphs. Which next experiment is most diagnostic?

options.text: Merge both languages into one large chunk so either wording appears in every result.
Raise top-k until a reviewer can find the matching language passage.
Translate every query to English and remove the original language from index metadata.
Compare language-specific and aligned retrieval using paired revision-aware queries.

prompt: An index build starts at generation 410. Before it publishes, a source is deleted and the active corpus advances to generation 411. The build succeeds and contains the deleted source. What publication guard is required?

options.text: Remove the source from the source store but leave the index active until the next scheduled rebuild.
Reject any manifest built before the current deletion generation.
Trust the build-start timestamp and assume later deletion events will be replayed automatically.
Publish because the vector build completed successfully and delete the old vector afterward.

prompt: A support answer cites a single sentence from a policy chunk. The sentence uses ‘it’ and ‘this plan’, while the preceding paragraph defines which plan those terms refer to. The answer is wrong for another plan. What change best addresses the retrieval failure?

options.text: Return the sentence with a confidence disclaimer and retain the current citation.
Ask the model to resolve pronouns using its general knowledge of plan names.
Retrieve the antecedent with the sentence and preserve the section path.
Add the question text to the embedding input so ‘this plan’ is more likely to match.

prompt: A policy team changes only a section heading from ‘Contractors’ to ‘Temporary staff’; the body text is unchanged. Retrieval examples suggest the new heading changes which questions find the section. Which evaluation is most useful before rebuilding the full index?

options.text: Compare only corpus-wide average similarity scores before and after the rename.
Replay role-specific queries against both headings and verify scope and citations.
Add both headings permanently to every chunk in the section.
Rebuild the index and ship because the body text has not changed.

prompt: A customer asks for a current warranty exception. Retrieval returns the correct paragraph from revision 8, while the active source manifest says revision 9 replaced it last week. The two revisions differ only in an adjacent exception table. What should the answer path do?

options.text: Fetch the active revision and its changed exception table before answering.
Use revision 8 because it is a direct paragraph match and the body appears unchanged.
Cite the revision 8 paragraph and mention that the source may have changed.
Combine revision 8’s paragraph with revision 9’s table to maximize context.

prompt: An index has chunks from both a procedure and its appendix. A question asks for a limit whose value appears in the appendix, but the procedure says the appendix applies only to devices sold after a stated date. The retriever returns the value without that condition. Which change tests the real failure?

options.text: Copy the limit into the procedure chunk during indexing.
Add the date condition to the query embedding as a synthetic prefix.
Retrieve the appendix value with its applicability condition and source link.
Increase top-k so the procedure might appear somewhere among additional chunks.

prompt: An HR knowledge index includes policy text plus a generated summary for each chunk. A query retrieves a summary that says ‘managers may approve exceptions’; the original passage says exceptions require a second approver. What should the answer system rely on?

options.text: Use the generated summary because it was created from the source and is shorter.
Combine both statements and say either approval path may apply.
Ask the model to infer whether a second approver is usually required.
Retrieve the eligibility definition with the refund exception and retain both citations.

prompt: A medical-device corpus has many short warning statements and a small number of long installation workflows. A query asks whether one warning applies during step 6 of a workflow. Which evaluation set best tests the chunking choice?

options.text: Narrow by product and version, then expand to linked procedure evidence as needed.
Use only frequent warning queries because they dominate production traffic.
Test only long workflows and ignore warning retrieval precision.
Use random chunks as queries and measure embedding similarity.

prompt: An invoice policy is represented as one text chunk per page. The refund exception begins on page 4, while the eligible-customer definition is on page 3; retrieval often returns only the exception. Which repair should be tested?

options.text: Index each page separately and ask the answer model to infer the eligibility rule from the refund amount.
Inspect the tenant’s active manifest and repair its generation-specific activation path.
Copy the customer definition into the exception text during indexing without recording its original source.
Increase overlap until most page-3 text is duplicated on page 4, then keep citations at page level.

prompt: A corpus has 2 million tokens of product manuals. Most questions identify a product and version; only a minority need a multi-section repair procedure. The current retriever embeds every paragraph in one flat namespace. What design is a useful next test?

options.text: Search all paragraphs globally, then rely on the model to discard other product versions from a large top-k.
Index only the repair procedures because those questions need the most context.
Embed entire manuals as single vectors so each product’s information remains together.
Use the current source passage as evidence and treat the generated summary as a locator.

prompt: A document owner approves a new retention rule, but the vector index still serves the previous rule for a subset of tenants. Logs show the source revision is current globally, while tenant manifests differ. What should the diagnosis inspect?

options.text: Rebuild the global index again because the global source revision is already current.
Increase retrieval top-k so the new and old rules are both returned for reconciliation.
Test standalone warnings and workflow-linked warnings with their conditions.
Use the newest global passage for every tenant until each tenant index catches up.

prompt: One internal service has a stable typed endpoint for checking a shipment. A second team now needs the same capability from Claude Desktop and Claude Code, with centrally managed server rollout and a discoverable schema. What change is justified?

options.text: Replace the typed service API with a shell script copied into each client.
Expose a governed MCP adapter for shared clients and keep the typed service backend.
Move the shipment capability to an agent-to-agent protocol so clients can delegate it.
Keep the one-off dashboard integration and let each new client reverse engineer its endpoint.

prompt: A nightly job transfers 8 million records with checkpoints, backpressure, and an existing streaming API. Analysts also ask Claude to inspect individual records interactively. Which integration split fits both workloads?

options.text: Have one agent call another agent for every record and stream the answers back.
Keep bulk transfer on its streaming API and use MCP for bounded interactive inspection.
Use a shell CLI for interactive Claude access and remove the streaming endpoint.
Send all eight million rows through MCP tool calls so both workloads use one protocol.

prompt: A tool server’s capabilities are stable, but its responses contain large records that users need only occasionally. The Claude client currently loads every record at session start. Which protocol design should be evaluated?

options.text: Place all records into tool descriptions so the model can choose without another call.
Create one agent per record and ask them to summarize everything at startup.
Return only record names forever and require users to open a separate system for every detail.
Load compact capability metadata and fetch authorized record bodies on demand.

prompt: A team proposes MCP for a single command that must run in cron with no network connection. The command has a stable local executable and no tool discovery or shared remote clients. Which choice is most proportionate?

options.text: Introduce a remote MCP server so cron can negotiate a capability it already invokes locally.
Convert the command to agent-to-agent messaging so it can be retried by another worker.
Embed the command’s entire output corpus in the prompt so the job is stateless.
Retain the local CLI for offline scheduling; add a server only for a real shared consumer.

prompt: A shared MCP server requires tenant-specific tools. The server filters tool calls by tenant, but its tools/list response exposes every tenant’s tool names and resource titles. What is the correct security review outcome?

options.text: Make every tenant’s tools globally callable so discovery and execution have matching behavior.
Hide only the tool descriptions while leaving names and resource titles visible.
Accept the design because actual calls and resource reads are denied across tenants.
Filter discovery by tenant and test both listings and execution authorization.

prompt: A connector is implemented as MCP, but it performs a long-running, multi-step research task and returns a narrative with delegated worker results. The implementation team reports that retries and partial worker completion are hard to reason about. What architecture review should happen first?

options.text: Increase the response timeout until all workers usually finish.
Add more MCP tools for every internal worker step and let the model decide when the workflow is complete.
Clarify whether the capability is a deterministic tool operation or an owned agent workflow, then assign orchestration and completion state to the appropriate layer.
Switch to an API for every worker call without changing workflow ownership.

prompt: A remote MCP server changes its resource schema during deployment while connected clients may hold older schema versions. A malformed result is rejected by one client but silently misread by another. What rollout control is most appropriate?

options.text: Remove schema validation so every client can accept the new response shape.
Deploy the schema change first and tell clients to retry if parsing fails.
Keep both schemas in one unversioned response and ask each client to guess which fields apply.
Version the schema and verify compatibility across representative clients before rollout.

prompt: A research coordinator asks three agents to independently investigate different sources, preserve evidence provenance, and return structured findings to a lead that synthesizes a report. The current design exposes each worker only as a deterministic MCP tool. What should the architect examine?

options.text: Separate the owned research workflow from the tools its workers use.
Keep the design and simply raise the token limit for the lead’s final prompt.
Replace the lead with one direct API call to a single source.
Expose every research step as an MCP resource so the lead can load all source contents at once.

prompt: A desktop assistant needs read-only access to a small, stable customer lookup. The organization already has a secure API, but users also want to inspect the available operation schema and the server owner wants one centrally controlled connector for several Claude clients. What should be proposed?

options.text: Use a narrow MCP adapter for shared Claude clients and retain the API boundary.
Replace the existing service with an agent that decides how to query customer records.
Give every client a copy of the API credentials and a hand-written prompt describing the endpoint.
Expose the entire database as a resource so no tool call is needed.

prompt: A batch pipeline must upload 2 TB nightly from a private network with resumable transfer and checksum verification. An architect suggests asking a Claude agent to split the files into tool calls. What is the strongest response?

options.text: Keep bulk movement on the resumable, checksum-verified data plane.
Use agent-to-agent delegation so multiple agents can upload separate fragments.
Use MCP because it gives every transfer step a discoverable name.
Send file contents in prompts and ask the model to confirm each checksum.

prompt: An MCP server declares `tools.listChanged` and loads an optional tool after an administrator enables a feature. Connected clients keep the old list, and the server emits no list-change notification. What should the team verify?

options.text: Keep the startup list immutable until every client reconnects, even when the server already supports list-change notification.
Refresh or renegotiate capabilities after the server’s enabled feature set changes.
Restart the server and advertise the tool to every tenant, including those where the feature remains disabled.
Tell the model the guessed tool name in a prompt while leaving the cached client capability list unchanged.

prompt: An MCP server exposes project files as resources. A request contains a `file://` URI outside the approved workspace, and the server process can read that path. Which boundary should the server enforce?

options.text: Expose the whole filesystem as one resource and instruct the assistant to use only project files.
Trust the client to list only approved resources, then read any syntactically valid URI it submits.
Enforce destination and resource authorization at the privileged server boundary.
Check that the URI parses and ask the model to decline any path that looks like a system file.

prompt: A route’s cost per attempt is $0.12 and it resolves 60% on the first try. A retry policy raises resolution to 84% but adds an average $0.10 for each initial failure; a second route costs $0.19 and resolves 90% on the first try. Which comparison is relevant to the stated goal of lowest spend per resolved case?

options.text: Compare full-policy cost per resolution, including retries, failures, and latency.
Compare only cost among successful first attempts.
Choose the $0.12 route because it has the lowest attempt price.
Choose the $0.19 route because its first-pass resolution is highest.

prompt: A long stable system prefix is reused frequently. Measurements show caching lowers cost but adds 120 ms; the route has 80 ms of remaining p95 budget. Quality is unchanged. What should the team conclude?

options.text: Discard the cache results because any additional latency makes caching unsuitable everywhere.
Test cache placement against this slice’s p95 budget and quality floor.
Enable caching only on half of traffic and call the route compliant based on average latency.
Enable caching because lower spend outweighs a small latency increase.

prompt: A structured extraction answer requires five fields. After prompt tuning, output tokens triple and p95 rises by 600 ms, while field accuracy is unchanged. Which next experiment is most direct?

options.text: Raise the timeout so the longer response can finish.
Switch to a cheaper model before inspecting the verbose output.
Truncate responses after the five field names appear.
Constrain output to required fields and measure validity, tokens, and route p95.

prompt: A retrieval route fans out to 20 sources for every request. Most cases need three sources; p95 rises above target and provider throttling grows. Which experiment preserves evidence quality while addressing the measured cause?

options.text: Switch to a smaller model to compensate for the extra retrieval cost.
Keep all 20 calls but make them parallel so their sum no longer affects latency.
Limit every request permanently to the top three sources without measuring recall.
Use query-aware bounded retrieval with a staged expansion when initial evidence is insufficient, then compare recall, p95, and 429 rate.

prompt: A candidate saves 25% per call but lowers premium contract review completeness from 94% to 81%; routine requests are unchanged. The quality floor is 90% for premium reviews. Which routing change should be evaluated?

options.text: Adopt the candidate everywhere because routine volume dominates aggregate quality.
Use the candidate for premium cases and add a disclaimer when fields are missing.
Route premium work to a configuration that meets its slice-specific floor.
Route every request to the expensive configuration to maximize one aggregate score.

prompt: One cache prefix is used once and incurs a write cost; another identical prefix receives many later reads. The current report pools all prefixes and shows savings. What analysis should guide policy?

options.text: Evaluate caching by prefix reuse count, full lifecycle cost, and route latency.
Enable cache globally because pooled spend is lower.
Compare cache-read token price alone with uncached token price.
Disable all cache use because some prefixes are read only once.

prompt: A smaller model is cheaper and faster on average, but a new traffic slice contains longer legal documents and has twice the tool-call rate. Overall cost rises after launch despite the lower model price. What should be examined first?

options.text: Decompose comparable slices by mix, retries, tokens, and cost per resolution.
Replace the new model with the most expensive model to improve tool accuracy.
Compare total daily spend without normalizing request volume or task type.
Roll back immediately because the provider must be charging more per token.

prompt: A retry policy increases average resolution from 82% to 89%, but the retries target malformed tool arguments that remain malformed on every attempt. Cost rises 18% and the hard p95 target is breached. What repair should be tested?

options.text: Drop the malformed calls from the denominator because they never reached the tool.
Retry at a higher model temperature to vary arguments until one works.
Increase retry count to recover more malformed calls.
Fix the argument contract and retry only plausibly transient failures.

prompt: A prompt-cache rollout reduces input spend by 22%, while p95 increases 250 ms. The route has a 300 ms margin, but a high-risk request slice has only 100 ms margin due to an extra validation stage. How should the rollout be evaluated?

options.text: Reject caching everywhere because it increases p95.
Remove the validation stage from high-risk requests to recover the budget.
Evaluate cache impact against each slice’s latency and quality constraints.
Roll out globally because the aggregate p95 increase fits inside the route-wide margin.

prompt: A report shows that parallelizing validation cut average latency by 400 ms. However, the verifier now runs before all evidence fetches finish on 7% of requests. Which release decision is justified?

options.text: Rerun the test only on requests where all fetches completed quickly.
Restore the evidence dependency before accepting the latency change.
Accept because 93% of requests preserve the original ordering and average latency improved.
Keep the early verifier and add a confidence disclaimer to affected answers.

prompt: A new route costs 12% less and has the same average answer score, but it misses the quality floor on the ‘urgent escalation’ slice. Overall traffic is 96% routine. Which optimization decision is defensible?

options.text: Route urgent cases to the cheaper model and add a human disclaimer after generation.
Accept the route globally because the overall average score is unchanged and urgent cases are rare.
Reject the lower-cost route for every case because it fails one slice.
Route by the quality floor of each request class and measure each slice.

prompt: An engineer shortens an output token cap and lowers cost, but 6% of structured responses now omit a required field. The route’s cost target is met and its completeness floor is 99%. What should happen next?

options.text: Raise the cap for every request to the former maximum and abandon output optimization.
Use schema-aware output control and preserve the required completeness floor.
Keep the cap because the average response still contains most required fields and cost is on target.
Fill missing fields with defaults after parsing so the response schema is complete.

prompt: Two model routes meet the same quality floor. Route A costs less per attempt but has p95 4.6 s; route B costs more but has p95 2.1 s. The product allows async completion up to 10 minutes for this batch job and has a fixed daily budget. Which evaluation is appropriate?

options.text: Compare both routes against a 3-second interactive p95 limit before considering the budget.
Choose A immediately because cost is the only hard constraint stated.
Choose B because the lower p95 is always better for any AI workload.
Compare total batch cost and quality under the budget, and verify that each route completes within the asynchronous deadline rather than applying an interactive p95 target.

prompt: A provider usage report provides hourly token totals by workspace and model. Finance asks which customer tickets caused a spend increase, but the report has no ticket IDs and multiple tickets run concurrently. What evidence should the team use?

options.text: Assign each ticket the provider’s workspace-hour total divided by ticket count.
Use model name as the ticket key because each workspace has one preferred model.
Use application-side request records with stable ticket-to-operation links and reconcile their measured usage to provider aggregates at supported time and workspace scope.
Join each ticket to the nearest provider timestamp and call that exact attribution.

prompt: The application error dashboard shows zero failures for one region. Its exporter heartbeat is stale, while load-balancer traffic continues normally. What should the incident view report?

options.text: Keep zero failures because no error spans arrived.
Copy load-balancer request totals into the application completion count.
Estimate failures from the prior region’s error percentage and label them as actual.
Mark route outcomes unknown, alert on exporter health, and keep edge traffic separate.

prompt: A cache dashboard reports a rise in cache-read tokens and a fall in total input tokens. A route’s answers are now less grounded, but the dashboard lacks prompt version and retrieval source IDs. What should be added to the diagnostic view?

options.text: Join prompt/index versions to sampled groundedness outcomes and request metrics.
Store all prompts and retrieved passages for every request indefinitely.
Track only total workspace tokens and infer route quality from spend.
Treat higher cache reads as proof that the correct prompt was reused.

prompt: A warm worker sometimes reuses a prior customer’s retrieval filter. Provider uptime and usage remain normal, and the application logs only aggregate request counts. What telemetry would most directly expose this defect while limiting sensitive data?

options.text: Trace opaque tenant binding through retrieval and validate it before delivery.
Add more provider token charts because a wrong filter may change token totals.
Log the full customer profile and every retrieved document for all requests.
Record only whether the final answer was returned successfully.

prompt: A cost dashboard combines provider usage and application retries, but its join duplicates one hourly provider total across every retry attempt. The resulting spend is several times higher than the invoice. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Keep the join and add a note that totals are approximate.
Replace provider totals with application retry counts as the cost measure.
Divide the duplicated amount by retry count to estimate exact cost per attempt.
Remove the unsupported many-to-one attribution, report provider totals once at their actual scope, and show retry counts separately until a valid request-level mapping exists.

prompt: A production panel shows stable completion rate and p95. A new reviewer sample reports unsupported citations in one document type, but quality labels arrive three days late. What operational view helps the team act without pretending the labels are current?

options.text: Combine the late labels with current requests and describe the result as live quality.
Keep provider totals at their supported grain and show retries separately.
Ignore groundedness until labels are available in real time.
Use completion rate as a substitute for citation support.

prompt: One route has normal workspace-level spend but unusually high retry volume in a single deployment. The provider Usage API groups by model and workspace, while application traces know route and release. Which join is defensible?

options.text: Assign the full workspace-model total to the deployment with the most retries.
Conclude that retries caused the spend increase because both rose in the same hour.
Join every retry to the workspace-hour total and sum the result.
Compare aggregate provider usage by its supported workspace/time/model dimensions with application retry counts by route/release, and label the comparison as correlated rather than request-exact.

prompt: An alert fires when daily workspace spend exceeds a fixed threshold. An approved launch doubles expected traffic, but the alert now pages continuously despite normal per-request economics. What should be changed?

options.text: Remove the spend alert because traffic has increased.
Alert only on provider availability and infer spend safety from uptime.
Show immediate delivery and delayed quality cohorts with freshness and coverage.
Raise the threshold until alerts stop without measuring the new workload baseline.

prompt: A release review dashboard compares one day of provider usage but seven days of application completions. The ‘cost per resolved case’ falls by 40%. What is the first correction?

options.text: Scale the one-day spend to seven days using the latest daily average.
Use the seven-day completion count with the one-day usage figure because completions are less volatile.
Accept the result because provider usage is a direct billing measure.
Compare like workspace/time/model dimensions and label route correlation as non-exact.
